Type.evidence_source: [page/5/Text/8] We recognize some of the traits described in these studies in our own material, but there are also significant differences and the descriptions provide a more nuanced picture of the elderly people.

Area.evidence_source: [page/5/Text/4] Nonetheless the majority became well-established as adults and emerged as vigorous and "achieving" people – many also in later life. They had been markedly actionoriented, even when loss and crises had occurred earlier in life. They seemed to maintain their pressing need to control into old age, and showed little ability to develop new strategies for adapting. [page/5/Text/8] Work had undoubtedly been important for them as a positive force in their lives. They were not afraid of responsibility, and many of them had shown creativity, competence, and considerable work capacity in their field. For many of them the work arena was also a social setting where they could make their contribution to others. The impression from the descriptions was that for them work was exactly that "pleasurable experience" where they found "fulfillment". They put demands on themselves and were very conscientious, but without this appearing forced. [page/6/Text/3] If we relate our findings to these control concepts, the informants tell us about people who had been capable of exercising strong primary control throughout their lives, and the experience of having control was important for their selfesteem. They also coped with loss earlier in life through primary control strategies. Whether they experienced loss of relationships or health at an early or a late age, work and activity was their remedy. [page/6/Text/7] These theoretical control perspectives can serve to give us an understanding of why elderly people with such "patterns" as those described by the informants will be particularly vulnerable when irreversible loss of functional capacity occurs in old age. Their self-image and self-esteem is associated with and dependent on the experience of control, exercised through strength and action. To be able to accept help they must let this control go, which they cannot do. For the same reason they are also unable to develop secondary control strategies. Closedoff feelings and relationships involving distance contribute to this. The overall result may be great loneliness, which further reinforces the pain of the loss of self-esteem. In his theory of "suicide as escape from self", Baumeister describes how loss of self-esteem can cause reactions that lead to the risk of suicide. He claims the starting-point may be that a person no longer manages to live up to his or her own expectations (Baumeister, 1990).
